Distinguished ministers, administrator of UNDP, Mr. Alexander Dekker, distinguished representatives of international organizations and financial institutions, ladies and gentlemen, It is a great pleasure to be here with you at this gathering in New York, which holds particular significance for us on the road to COP31. I respectfully greet each and every one of you and welcome you to the launch of the Climate Implementation Bridge. Distinguished participants, we have not gathered today merely to launch a new initiative. We are jointly seeking an answer to one of the most fundamental questions facing climate action. How will we bring the commitments we have made together with our country's development priorities, and how will we turn them into actionable investments and tangible results on the ground? Yes, over the past decade, the international community has made significant efforts to strengthen climate targets. countries have prepared and updated their nationally determined contributions. They have developed adaptation plans, long-term low emission development strategies and sectoral transformation targets. Now we have another responsibility before us, implementation. We must now discuss not only which targets we will set, but also how we will implement these targets on the ground. As I stated in Bonn, while developing the COP31 Action Agenda, we focused on the world's most urgent needs, the implementation challenges faced by countries on the ground, and the areas where COP31 can make a lasting contribution. Because The world needs not a new list of commitments, but the transformation of existing commitments into concrete results. As a COP31 presidency, we have therefore built our journey towards Antalya around three fundamental principles: dialogue, consensus and action. Dialogue enables us to understand different national circumstances and needs. Consensus enables us to come together around common solutions. Action, meanwhile, transforms our targets into concrete results in people's lives, in our cities and in our economies. We are developing the Climate Implementation Bridge with this understanding. Throughout our preparatory process, we have conducted extensive consultations with countries, United Nations organizations, multilateral development banks, international financial institutions, climate funds and representatives of the private sector. These consultations have given us a clear picture. Many countries know what they need to do. They have their climate targets, development priorities and sectoral strategies. However, they face significant challenges in turning these priorities into actionable investment programs and projects into financing and concrete results. On the other hand, significant technical and financial support capacity exists. The United Nations system, development banks, climate funds, international financial institutions, bilateral partners, and the private sector offer important opportunities. However, these opportunities do not always meet countries' priorities at the right time and in the right way. BRIDGE aims to respond precisely to this gap. We want to bring climate targets together more effectively with national development priorities and financing opportunities. We want to identify bottlenecks to implementation, strengthen countries' investment readiness, and enable them to make more effective use of existing international support ecosystem. Here, I would like to underline an important point. BRIDGE is not a new fund, a new financing mechanism or a new structure intended as an alternative to existing institutions. It is a country-focused initiative that starts from countries' own priorities and existing national systems and aims to bring existing capacities and support opportunities together more effectively around implementation. Our goal is to transform commitments into implementation, implementation into investment, and investment into concrete results. Today, we are reaching an important stage in this journey. We are pleased to welcome the first group of countries. Ethiopia, Fiji, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Uzbekistan will be the first group of countries to begin working with BRIDGE. We will keep increasing the number of these countries in the upcoming term. We do not see these countries merely as countries that will benefit from BRIDGE. Their experiences, needs and feedback will also directly contribute to shaping how BRIDGE develops. Because we see BRIDGE as an initiative shaped not only for countries, but also together with countries. implementation requires strong partnerships. For this reason, we attach great importance to the partnership we have established with the United Nations Development Programme, and I would like to extend my gratitude to them before you, because they have really owned this subject since day one, and they worked very hard along with our team. The global expertise of the United Nations system and UNDP, its strong presence at the country level and its work under Climate Promise Forward will make an important contribution to transforming BRIDGE into a structure that responds to the country's needs. I would like to thank United Nations Development Programme for this partnership and its strong support. Another fundamental element of implementation is finance. Climate finance is not an end in itself for us. It is the bridge between commitments and results. At the Climate Finance Summit we held in Istanbul on 4th of September, we strongly conveyed this message together with the governments, multilateral development banks, international financial institutions and investors. Today, We're taking this call one step further from New York. We invite governments, international organizations, development banks, climate funds, investors, and the private sector to build partnerships for implementation. As we move towards Antalya, our objective is not merely to launch an initiative. We want to make concrete progress with our first countries, bring new countries into the process, strengthen the participation of finance and development actors, and leave a lasting legacy that will continue to serve countries' implementation efforts beyond COP31. And in Antalya, while advancing the action agenda and our work on implementation, we know that strong implementation on the ground must advance together with international cooperation, trust and strong consensus at the negotiating table. And I believe the Climate Implementation Bridge will be one of the concrete tools of this approach. and we will focus on bringing countries' priorities together with international support capacity in a more effective manner. And today here in New York, we are taking an important step on this path together. I would like to thank especially UNDP, as well as all the other countries, for taking this step. in order to fill the gap between implementation and finance. Financing then follows to implementation on the ground. The dashed lines close the loop, our results and learning return to the Belém Mission, scaling and replication to the Accelerator. On the right, the COP31 presidency and the Global Bridge Steering Committee constitute the governing body. At the country level, the process runs from entry to exit. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, let me begin by expressing our appreciation to COP31 presidency for convening this timely discussion on the climate implementation bridge. With the full operationalization of the Paris Agreement at COP29, including the agreement on new collective quantified goal and Article 6, we have now entered what is increasingly described as implementation era. Over the past years, we have developed ambitious climate commitments, including NDCs, NAPs and long-term strategies. Well-prepared climate plans are essential to showcase intention for translating commitments under the Paris Agreement into action. But submission alone is not enough. Ambitious plans must be followed by robust implementation, investment and institutional action to deliver meaningful results. For many developing countries, the availability and accessibility of finance, the shortage of finance-ready and bankable projects, a limited institutional capacity to prepare and implement them remain significant challenges. This makes the link between climate ambition, development planning, and finance particularly important. In this context, a climate implementation bridge offers a practical framework to better align climate goals with economic decision-making improve access to finance, and accelerate implementation. Importantly, BRIDGE is not intended to create a new financing mechanism, implementation agency, or coordination platform. Rather, it seeks to strengthen the effectiveness and connectivity of existing institutions, initiatives, and support mechanisms, helping countries address key implementation challenges and translate climate ambition into action. In this context, we particularly welcome the emphasis of BRIDGE on building on existing initiatives and support platforms rather than creating parallel structures. In this context, we see an important connection between Climate Implementation BRIDGE and the Baku Initiative for Climate Finance, Investment and Trade, or BICFIT dialogue, launched under COP29 presidency. While BRIDGE focuses on connecting national climate priorities with development planning, investment and financing opportunities, BIGFIT brings together the climate finance, investment and trade communities to support national climate ambitions and sustainable investment. Both initiatives therefore contribute to the same practical objective, connecting national climate priorities with the financial, investment and economic systems needed to turn them into implementable action. We see considerable potential for these approaches to complement and reinforce each other. In conclusion, we look forward to continuing this conversation with the COP31 presidency and all partners and to advancing the objectives of the BRIDGE initiative. Thank you.
